To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) performance-avoidance goals are associated with negative affect, (b) performance-approach and mastery goals are associated with positive affect, and (c). performance-avoidance and mastery goals are unrelated.

performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals are positively associated with each other and with mastery-avoidance goals, and that mastery-approach goals are negatively related to mastery-avoidance and performance-avoid goals.

performance-approach goal orientations are not necessarily harmful, that mastery-approach goal orientation is not necessarily beneficial, that mastery-avoidance and performance-avoidance goal orientations are detrimental, and that the relative effects of these goal orientations are moderated by situational and dispositional factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of different goal orientations on the development of adaptive and maladaptive achievement behaviors in different achievement contexts and with the implications for the promotion of adaptive achievement behavior.
the effects of mastery goals and performance-approach and avoidance goals on students' motivation and achievement.
the question of what makes achievement contexts optimal for students.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mastery-approach goals are always good, performance-approach goal are always bad, and mastery-avoidance goals are always bad.
the theory is in need or revision, but not that it is wrong.
performance-approach and mastery goals can be beneficial or detrimental to motivation, learning, or achievement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is necessary to revise the theory and research on achievement goals to accommodate the complexity of the motivational processes in different achievement contexts.
the authors have contributed to the development of achievement goal theory and have helped to clarify the theoretical assumptions and empirical evidence that underlie the theory.
we have contributed to a better understanding of achievement goals in the classroom.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should not be afraid to ask critical questions about the assumptions and interpretations of theory and to challenge the status quo.

the theory needs to be revised to account for a broader range of motivational phenomena and to provide a more complete explanation of the conditions under which performance-approach and mastery goals can be adaptive and maladaptive (Midgley et al., 2002).
we need a more complex theory that can account for both positive and negative outcomes associated with performance-approach goal orientations.
